functional_compartments.function_note: Hooks around the dorsal (Lister's) tubercle of the radius -- a documented bones.json landmark -- changing its line of pull, unlike APL/EPB which run straight to the thumb.

trigger_points.location_description: Not mapped by Travell and Simons; the source document infers a taut band in the EPL belly in the deep dorsal forearm distal to abductor pollicis longus. [clinical reasoning]
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Dorsal thumb and dorsoradial wrist pain is inferred; the documented remote sources of dorsal thumb pain are supinator (dorsal thumb web and proximal thumb) and brachialis (base of thumb). [clinical reasoning -- not a Travell & Simons figure for EPL itself]
trigger_points.notes: Non-myofascial differential: EPL tenosynovitis or rupture, distal intersection syndrome, dorsal wrist ganglion, scapholunate injury, basal-joint arthritis, C6 radiculopathy.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons (1999) Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed., Vol. 1; Donnelly et al. (2019) 3rd ed. -- no distinct EPL figure exists in either edition; pattern is labelled [clinical reasoning] in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference.

Bracketed numbers point to the master list in Appendix B; every profile ends with its own reference list. Claims that could not be tied to a verified source are labelled [clinical reasoning] or [UNVERIFIED]. Appendix A grades the match between each key claim and its source.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Extension of the thumb IP joint (assisted by the intrinsic expansions), then MCP and carpometacarpal extension; adduction and retropulsion of the thumb (lifting the thumb dorsal to the plane of the palm, the EPL-specific test) with supination of the thumb ray [1, 5, 6]. At the wrist: Weak wrist extension and radial deviation [1, 6]. Importance: Reconstructed after rupture by EI-to-EPL transfer; 3rd compartment release and tendon transposition are routine in dorsal approaches to the distal radius [4].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: Narrow 3rd compartment synovial sheath; no bursa [1]. Relations: Lister's tubercle, the dorsal rim of the distal radius (fracture callus, dorsal plates), ECRL/ECRB tendons at the distal intersection, radial artery in the snuffbox [1, 51, 52]. Coupled structures: Lister's tubercle (pulley), 3rd compartment, distal radius, ECRL/ECRB tendons, thumb extensor hood with APB and adductor pollicis [1].

trigger_points.referred_pain: Not mapped by Travell and Simons. A taut band in the EPL belly (deep dorsal forearm, distal to APL) produces dorsal thumb and dorsoradial wrist pain; the documented remote sources of dorsal thumb pain are supinator (dorsal thumb web and proximal thumb) and brachialis (base of thumb) [clinical reasoning] [2, 3].

clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred into EPL territory (dorsal thumb, dorsoradial wrist)
clinical.non_myofascial_differential: EPL tenosynovitis or rupture, distal intersection syndrome, dorsal wrist ganglion, scapholunate injury, basal-joint arthritis, C6 radiculopathy.
clinical.notes: Delayed attritional rupture after distal radius fracture, typically weeks after minimally displaced fractures, is attributed to the hypovascular tendon zone combined with mechanical attrition and raised pressure in the intact 3rd compartment [51, 52]; rupture also follows dorsal plating and rheumatoid synovitis. Repetitive wrist extension and thumb use can cause 3rd compartment tenosynovitis ("drummer boy" palsy). Distal intersection syndrome involves the EPL crossing of ECRL/ECRB [4].
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
